newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya maximises coffee sales as shortage persists.
newsitem.headline: Kenya maximises coffee sales as shortage persists.

text.p: Kenya plans to sell as much coffee as comes through its weekly auctions during the current period of a world shortage of quality coffee.

A senior official at the Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd, a subsidiary of the regulatory and marketing authority Coffee Board of Kenya, told Reuters on Monday a world shortage of quality arabica coffees meant that Kenyan coffees would still be sought by roasters. Any possibility of export quotas would not be applicable.
"We've got to wait and see how it develops. There is a global shortage and we can't do anything about that. In any case our crop is too small for any quotas," the official said.

Coffee producers are holding two days of talks in London this week against a backdrop of a surge in coffee prices which took U.S. arabica futures to a 20-year high last week. Some of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' 14 members want to suspend their programme of export quotas.
A trader in Nairobi said that the possibility of roasters shifting to robusta coffees did not bother many arabica producers.
"Certainly, some roasters may want to lower the quality of their blends to make safeguard profits and to keep afloat.
"People have tried to fiddle with blends over time. That has now been exhausted, we don't know whether the blends can be taken any lower than has been done," a coffee dealer said.
One trader said a failure of seasonal short rains (Oct-Dec) in Kenya and the subsequent drought that persisted until late March meant significant damage to the "fly" mid-crop.

Kenya normally harvests around 28,000-30,000 tonnes of the mid crop. The coffee board put its estimate for the "fly" crop in 1996/97 (Oct/Sept) at 27,000 tonnes before the drought. Now drought damage will reduce that to 20,000-23,000 tonnes or further, a senior trader told Reuters.

Another official from the Kenya Coffee Auctions Ltd said there were worse figures of a failed crop, with "wild estimates such as only 15,000 tonnes. We have never dipped below 20,000 tonnes before but there is always a first time".
The Coffee Board of Kenya has offered around 35,000 60-kg bags of coffee for sale so far at the auctions. The board has said that will drop to 30,000 bags through June auctions.

Auctions officials estimated that figure will be lower, at around 28,000 bags through June. "We really do not know yet, that figure could be as low as 25,000 bags depending on the amount of coffee coming from the fields," one said.
"We anticipate less coffee coming through the system. Farmers have started to pick the 'fly' crop in some areas and there is talk that it is drought-affected," a trader said.

"We may not have enough of the main crop at end June and the 'fly crop' may be delayed in coming in, so we could see a very thin market in July. But even if the 'fly' crop makes it in time, it will be small. Either way, there is a shortage."

Traders said that on average they expected prices at this week's export auction on Tuesday to be higher outright than last week. But they added that differentials against New York would perhaps be lower.
"Last week we were around 200 (U.S.) cents over ordinary Central American coffees. I am not sure we can make any higher than that. We could ease a little," one said.

The coffee board estimates that 1996/97 production will at the most reach 80,000 tonnes compared to a final figure of 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95. Some dealers have put the 1996/97 crop at 75,000-78,000 tonnes.
